title: Indexed Aggregation: Stream vs Hash Aggregate
description: A GROUP BY with no supporting index uses a Hash Aggregate; an index in group order enables a cheaper Stream Aggregate. Why it matters: GROUP BY reporting queries are everywhere in business software, and this is a reliable, repeatable way to make them dramatically cheaper.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Picture sorting a big pile of receipts into stacks by store name so you can total up spending per store. If the receipts are in a totally random order, you'd have to build every stack from scratch as you go, constantly checking "do I already have a stack for this store, or do I need to start a new one?" That's slow and memory-hungry. But if the receipts were already handed to you sorted by store name, you could just walk through them once, adding to a running total, and the moment the store name changes you know that stack is finished and can move to the next. This lesson is about that exact difference, applied to SQL Server's `GROUP BY`.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** `GROUP BY` is how you ask a database to summarize data — "total sales per region," "count of orders per customer," things like that. Under the hood, SQL Server has two fundamentally different ways to actually perform that grouping, called a Hash Aggregate and a Stream Aggregate, and which one it picks depends entirely on whether the data arriving at the grouping step is already sorted by the group-by column.

**Why this happens in real databases.** By default, rows in a table aren't stored in any particular order relevant to an arbitrary `GROUP BY` you happen to write — a table might be physically ordered by its primary key, which has nothing to do with, say, grouping by `RegionId`. Without any help, SQL Server has to bring together all the rows belonging to the same group itself, wherever they happen to be scattered, before it can produce a total for that group. Whether that's cheap or expensive depends entirely on whether there's an index that already happens to store the data pre-sorted in group order.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** A Hash Aggregate works like this: as each row streams in, SQL Server computes a "hash" of the group-by column's value (a quick scrambled fingerprint used purely to organize the data) and uses it to find or create a bucket in memory for that group, then updates a running total in that bucket. Because rows can arrive in any order, this approach has to keep every group's running total available in memory simultaneously, updating whichever bucket a given row belongs to, until every row has been processed and every bucket has its final total. This works, but it needs memory proportional to the number of distinct groups, and if there turn out to be far more distinct groups than expected (again, often due to a bad estimate), it can spill to tempdb just like a sort can.

A Stream Aggregate, on the other hand, only works if the incoming rows already arrive in group-by order — meaning all the rows for group A arrive together, then all of group B, then all of group C, with no groups interleaved. If that's guaranteed, SQL Server can process the data in a single, efficient pass: keep a running total for "the current group," and the instant the group-by column's value changes, that's the signal the previous group is complete — emit its final total immediately and start a fresh running total for the new group. This needs almost no extra memory (it's only ever tracking one group's running total at a time) and no hashing overhead at all. The only way to guarantee rows arrive in that order cheaply is for there to be an index whose key order matches (or starts with) the `GROUP BY` columns — walking that index naturally produces exactly the sorted-by-group order the Stream Aggregate needs, with no separate sort step required.

**Why this matters in production.** `GROUP BY` reporting queries — totals, counts, summaries — are everywhere in business software: dashboards, monthly reports, "top customers," "sales by category." Without a supporting index, every one of these queries defaults to a Hash Aggregate, which not only uses more memory but, on a large enough table with a poorly estimated number of distinct groups, can spill to tempdb exactly the way a large sort can, dragging down not just this query but everything else sharing tempdb at the time. Because the query still returns correct results either way, this rarely raises alarms until the table has grown large enough for the difference to become painfully visible — a report that used to run in under a second suddenly taking many seconds as the underlying data scales up. In the execution plan, the tell is a Hash Match (Aggregate) operator instead of a Stream Aggregate; adding an index in group-by order flips the plan to the cheaper Stream Aggregate and, often, removes a separate Sort operator at the same time, since the index supplies the order the aggregate needs for free.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below runs a `GROUP BY` against a table with no supporting index, and shows you the Hash Match (Aggregate) operator SQL Server falls back to. After adding an index whose key order matches the `GROUP BY` columns, re-run the same query and watch the plan switch to a Stream Aggregate, often with any separate Sort operator disappearing at the same time — direct evidence that the index is delivering the rows already sorted, exactly the order the aggregate needs to process them in a single efficient pass.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** The same Hash-versus-Stream distinction shows up for `DISTINCT` and for some join strategies, not only explicit `GROUP BY` — anywhere SQL Server needs to bring matching values together, having them arrive pre-sorted (via an index) versus arriving in arbitrary order (requiring a hash-based structure) is the same underlying trade-off. It's also worth noting that a Hash Aggregate isn't automatically bad — for a query touching a small table, or one run only occasionally, the extra memory and hashing overhead may not matter at all; this pattern is worth chasing specifically when the query is frequent, the table is large, or the aggregate is visibly spilling to tempdb.

## Scenario
`SELECT CustomerId, COUNT(*), SUM(Total) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerId` aggregates 300,000 rows into ~3,000 customer groups. The plan scans the clustered index and finishes with a **Hash Match** aggregate.

## Why it's slow
A **Hash Match (Aggregate)** builds an in-memory hash table with one bucket per group and requires a **memory grant** up front. If the server is under memory pressure — or the optimizer underestimates the group count — that grant can be too small and the aggregate **spills to tempdb**, turning a CPU operation into disk I/O. There's nothing ordered by `CustomerId` for SQL Server to exploit, so hashing is its only option.

## What to look for
- A **Hash Match** operator (logical *Aggregate*) at the top of the plan.
- A full **Clustered Index Scan** feeding it, because no index is ordered by the grouping column.

## The concept
Give the optimizer a stream **already ordered by the GROUP BY column**. Create a nonclustered index on `CustomerId` (INCLUDE `Total` so it also covers the `SUM`). Now SQL Server reads the ordered index and uses a **Stream Aggregate**: because equal keys are adjacent, it collapses each group in a single pass with no hash table and no memory grant — immune to aggregate spills.
startingQuery: SELECT CustomerId, COUNT(*) AS Cnt, SUM(Total) AS TotalSum FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerId;
hints: A Hash Match aggregate is chosen when nothing feeds the GROUP BY in sorted order.
A Stream Aggregate needs its input pre-sorted on the grouping key -- what provides sorted order for free?
Create a nonclustered index on CustomerId and INCLUDE (Total) so it also covers the SUM.
